newsitem.title: UK: The minority view - EMU won't fly in 1999.
newsitem.headline: The minority view - EMU won't fly in 1999.

text.p: European markets have a big shock coming in 1997 if single currency sceptics are proved right.

Long-term interest rates in Europe have converged at a rapid pace all year as investors bet states from Sweden to Italy would take part in the planned economic and monetary union (EMU). Some analysts are starting to say a sour aftertaste is on the way.
"The party is over," said David Brown, chief international economist at Bear Stearns in London. "Convergence is dead."
The reality, some analysts say, is that Europe's single currency just won't get off the ground in 1999.
President Bill Clinton's 1992 election rallying cry "It's the economy, stupid!" fits snugly, and perversely, into the EMU doubters' argument.
They say the path to EMU has been laid on the unwavering political will of France and Germany, ignoring the economic realities that could tear a single currency structure apart.
"We expect things to start to go wrong in the second half of next year," said Robert Pryor, international economist at HSBC James Capel in London.

"People will begin to realise the Maastricht criteria must be taken seriously, and realise they will not be met," he said of the tough targets for monetary union set in the European Union's Maastricht treaty. Analysts identified a series of potential risks to the EMU programme, any one of which could undermine the single currency's planned structure and spark dramatic deconvergence among European debt yields.

Prospects for economic activity in core European countries would be the main problem, with slow gross domestic product (GDP) growth in Germany and France next year, when countries wishing to join EMU in 1999 must prove their worthiness.
"There is a lot of misplaced optimism that German growth is going all the way to 2.5-to-3.0 percent in 1997," said Brown.
But with high German unemployment capping consumer spending and the fiscal handcuffs slapped on governments by Maastricht, growth at this rate is unlikely to materialise, analysts said.
"There is a severe risk the German recovery will belly-flop as it did back in 1991-93," said Brown.
Stephen Bell, chief economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London, said that although EMU was still more likely to happen than not, he was becoming far more sceptical.
"Anyone who says EMU is a certainty is ignoring the economics, but anyone who says that EMU is never going to happen is ignoring the politics."

Like others, Bell pointed to France and Germany as the main stumbling blocks, saying public opposition in both countries was likely to heat up as the effects of tight budget packages started to squeeze people's spending power.
The damaging truckers' strike in France, now in its 11th day and triggered by budget measures to trim state pensions, was a case in point.
Bell said more social unrest was likely to come.
"The French government is more unpopular than any government since German occupation," he said in a reference to World War Two.
Cracks were also starting to appear in the Franco-German alliance, analysts said.

Bank of France council member Jean-Pierre Gerard, calling for a a weaker franc against the dollar, on Thursday said German lack of undertanding on monetary and exchange rate policy may make a change in the mark-franc parity necessary.

"The French economy is in trouble, the government is fast losing its patience and looking for fast remedies now," said Brown. "It could very quickly lose its tether on franc fort and start looking for extra growth leverage via a weaker franc."
But this would suggest a weaker euro and upset the Germans.
A further potential glitch would emerge from the so-called "Club Med" economies of Italy and Spain.
"Germany is very reluctant for these countries to be eligible for EMU (in 1999)," said Capel's Pryor. "But the difficulty may well be how to exclude these countries while keeping France in."
"Spain looks as though it will do as well as France and it may be impossible at the end of the day to seperate the two."

With EMU's top twins France and Germany struggling to meet the Maastricht criteria themselves, the majority view is that political determination will have to be relied upon to push for a 1999 birth date for the euro.
"The markets' assumption is that the politicians will force EMU through," said Pryor.
But relying on political will could cause a vicious circle.

The thinking goes something like this. If politics are the driving force, there could be a weakening of the EMU criteria. If the criteria are weakened and cuntries that are not fit are allowed in, the euro would emerge as a soft currency. And if the currency is expected to be too soft, public opinion may turn against EMU.
